grades.quote: members of the exec family return only if an error occurs; if all is well, the new program has started running, replacing the old program within the process, and so there is no possibility of returning in the old program.
grades.reason: Directly explains why executing in the shell itself would replace the shell rather than return to it.

grades.quote: A common example is fork followed by exec: a few pages may be written after the fork, but then the child’s exec releases the bulk of the memory inherited from the parent.
grades.reason: Provides auxiliary information about fork-then-exec efficiency, not why the shell must remain separate.

grades.quote: The child calls close and dup to make file descriptor zero refer to the read end of the pipe, closes the file descriptors in p, and calls exec to run wc. When wc reads from its standard input, it reads from the pipe. The parent closes the read side of the pipe, writes to the pipe, and then closes the write side.
grades.reason: Illustrates a child executing a command while the parent continues independently, but does not explain exec’s replacement semantics.

grades.quote: This leaves only the other big use of `fork` : creating a child process to run an entirely different program. In this case, the child code in the forking program is only long enough to load in the new program and start it running. This happens, for example, every time you type a program’s name at a shell prompt; the shell forks off a child process in which it runs the program.
grades.reason: Explains the shell’s fork-and-execute arrangement, but not explicitly why replacing the shell itself would prevent its continuation.
